title: Why Is There Water in My Dryer Vent?
h1: Why Is There Water in My Dryer Vent?
description: Water in a dryer vent usually comes from condensation in a long, cold or sagging run, a lint clog or rain getting past a broken cap. Here is how to fix it.
quick_answer: Water in a dryer vent is usually condensation. Hot, damp air from the dryer cools as it travels through the vent, and the moisture turns back to water, especially in long runs, cold attics or sagging sections. Lint clogs make it worse, and a broken or missing exterior cap can let rain in.
body:
Your dryer removes water from your clothes by turning it into steam and blowing it outside. If that warm, wet air slows down or cools off before it leaves, some of the moisture condenses inside the vent. A little condensation can happen in any vent. Standing water, drips at the dryer or rust stains are signs of a problem.

What causes water in a dryer vent?

  • Condensation in cold sections. Vents that run through an attic, crawl space or exterior wall can get cold, especially on cool nights inland or damp coastal mornings. Warm exhaust hits the cold duct and condenses.
  • A long vent run. The longer the air travels, the more it cools and the slower it moves, so more water drops out.
  • Sagging or low spots. Flexible duct and poorly supported metal duct can sag. Water collects in the low points.
  • Lint buildup. Lint slows airflow and soaks up moisture, which leaves wet, heavy clumps in the vent.
  • A broken or missing exterior cap. Without a working flap, rain and wind can blow into the vent.
  • Roof vents. Roof caps that are damaged, poorly flashed or the wrong type can let rain in, and water runs back down the vent.
  • Too many turns. Each elbow slows the air and gives moisture a place to settle.

Why is water in the vent a problem?

Wet lint sticks to the duct walls and builds up faster than dry lint, which leads to clogs. Water can rust metal duct, soak into drywall and framing, and lead to mold in the wall or attic. It also means your dryer is working harder and taking longer, and a clogged vent is a fire risk.

If you notice water dripping from the dryer itself, it's often water that ran back down the vent from a low spot or the cap.

How can I tell where the water is coming from?

  1. Check the weather. If water only shows up after rain, look at the exterior cap or roof vent.
  2. Check the cap. Make sure the flap opens when the dryer runs and closes fully when it stops. Look for cracks or missing pieces.
  3. Check airflow. With the dryer running, feel the air at the cap. Weak airflow points to a clog or crushed duct.
  4. Look for sags. If you can safely see the vent in the attic or behind the dryer, look for low spots and loose joints.
  5. Check the duct material. Foil or vinyl flex duct sags and traps water. It should be replaced with rigid metal.

How do I fix water in my dryer vent?

The fix depends on the cause:

  • Clean the vent to remove wet lint and restore airflow.
  • Replace sagging flex duct with smooth, rigid metal duct, properly supported with a steady slope toward the outside where possible.
  • Shorten or reroute a long or twisty vent run.
  • Insulate vent sections that pass through cold attics or crawl spaces to reduce condensation.
  • Replace a damaged cap with one that has a working flap and no screen.
  • Fix roof cap flashing if water is getting in at the roof.

Don't try to fix it by poking holes in the vent to let water drain. That lets lint and moisture escape into walls or the attic.

Does it matter what type of dryer I have?

Yes. Vented gas and electric dryers both create moist exhaust. Gas dryers also produce combustion gases, so their vents have to be sealed and clear at all times. Ventless or condensing dryers don't use an outside vent, so if you have one and see water, the issue is in the dryer's own water tank or drain hose, which is an appliance repair.

When should I call for help?

Call if you see standing water, water stains on walls or ceilings near the vent, rust on the duct, or water dripping back into the dryer. Also call if your vent runs through the attic or roof, since those are harder to inspect safely.

faqs: Is some condensation in a dryer vent normal?
A small amount can happen, especially in cold weather. Standing water, drips back into the dryer, rust or wet lint clumps are not normal and point to a slow, sagging, clogged or poorly capped vent.
Can I keep using my dryer if there is water in the vent?
It's best to have it checked soon. Water usually means poor airflow or a clog, which raises the fire risk and slows drying. Clean the lint screen and check the outside cap in the meantime.
Should a dryer vent be insulated?

Sections that pass through cold attics, crawl spaces or unheated areas can benefit from insulation to cut down on condensation. Insulation doesn't replace a short, straight, clean run, but it helps in colder spots.
Why is water dripping out of my dryer?
With a vented dryer, it's often condensation running back down the vent from a low spot, a long cold run or a leaky cap. With a ventless dryer, check the water tank and drain hose.
